title: Galois-stable subspaces of a scalar extension descend
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $L/k$ be an algebraic normal separable field extension [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension] (not necessarily finite), and put $\Gamma=\operatorname{Aut}_k(L)$. Let $M$ be any $k$-vector space and form $M_L=M\otimes_k L$, with its $L$-vector space structure on the second tensor factor [def-weil-module-base-change, def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. For $\sigma\in\Gamma$, define $\sigma_M(m\otimes\lambda)=m\otimes\sigma(\lambda)$ and extend additively. Let $W\subseteq M_L$ be an $L$-linear subspace such that $\sigma_M(W)=W$ for every $\sigma$. Define $W_0=\{m\in M:m\otimes1\in W\}$, a $k$-linear subspace of $M$. Then the $L$-linear map $W_0\otimes_kL\to M_L$, $w\otimes\lambda\mapsto w\otimes\lambda$, is injective and has image exactly $W$. Equivalently, it induces an isomorphism $W_0\otimes_kL\xrightarrow{\sim}W$. There is no finite-dimensionality assumption on $M$ or $W$.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581: continuous semilinear vector-space descent, restricted to a stable subspace of the canonical scalar-extension action; A.65 applies it to a defining ideal.

proof.text: Put $\iota(m)=m\otimes1$. Bilinearity makes $\iota$ $k$-linear, so $W_0=\iota^{-1}(W)$ is a $k$-subspace. The tensor universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] gives $F:W_0\otimes_kL\to M\otimes_kL$, $w\otimes\lambda\mapsto w\otimes\lambda$; its formula makes it $L$-linear. Its image is the $L$-span $N$ of $\iota(W_0)$: pure tensors generate the domain and $F(w\otimes\lambda)=\lambda\iota(w)$. Thus $N\subseteq W$ because $W$ is $L$-linear.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581 (descent assertion); the finite-support proof below is written by the agent, not the Morita-equivalence proof in A.64.

proof.text: Choose a $k$-basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of $M$ using [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-basis-through-vector] with the empty prescribed set. By the basis clause of [def-weil-vector-space-scalar-extension], $(e_i\otimes1)_{i\in I}$ is an $L$-basis of $M_L$. Write $x=\sum_i e_i\otimes c_i$ in these unique, finitely supported coordinates, and let $s(x)=\{i:c_i\ne0\}$. The formula for the action gives $\sigma_M(x)=\sum_i e_i\otimes\sigma(c_i)$. In particular $s(\sigma_M(x))=s(x)$, since field automorphisms take nonzero elements to nonzero elements.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581 (descent assertion); the finite-support proof below is written by the agent, not the Morita-equivalence proof in A.64.

proof.text: Fix a nonzero $x\in W$ and put $S=s(x)$. Among nonzero $u\in W$ with $s(u)\subseteq S$, choose one whose support has least cardinality (the set is nonempty because it contains $x$). Pick $p\in s(u)$ and divide $u$ by its nonzero $p$-coordinate, so that $c_p(u)=1$. For any $\sigma\in\Gamma$, the vector $\sigma_M(u)-u$ lies in $W$, has support contained in $s(u)$, and has zero $p$-coordinate. Minimality forces it to be zero. Uniqueness of coordinates therefore gives $\sigma(c_i(u))=c_i(u)$ for all $i$ and $\sigma$. Apply [lem-exc-etale-galois-fixed-field-subgroup] with its top extension $K=L$ and its intermediate field equal to the base field $k$: the subgroup fixing that intermediate field is all of $\Gamma$, so its fixed field is $k$. (The hypotheses are precisely the algebraic, normal and separable hypotheses on $L/k$.) Thus $c_i(u)=a_i\in k$; only finitely many $a_i$ are nonzero. Bilinearity gives $u=(\sum_i a_ie_i)\otimes1$. Since $u\in W$, the vector $\sum_i a_ie_i$ is in $W_0$ and $u\in N$. This argument applies to every nonzero $x\in W$ and supplies a vector $u\in N\cap W$ supported inside $s(x)$, with one specified coordinate $p$ equal to $1$.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581 (descent assertion); the finite-support proof below is written by the agent, not the Morita-equivalence proof in A.64.

proof.text: Prove $W\subseteq N$ by strong induction on $|s(x)|$ for $x\in W$. Empty support means $x=0\in N$. Otherwise take the vector $u$ and index $p$ just constructed. If $b$ is the $p$-coordinate of $x$, then $y=x-bu\in W$ has support contained in $s(x)\setminus\{p\}$: both vectors are supported in $s(x)$ and the $p$-coordinate cancels. Hence the induction hypothesis gives $y\in N$, and $x=y+bu\in N$ since $u\in N$ and $N$ is $L$-linear. Consequently $\operatorname{im}(F)=N=W$.

source.place: Appendix A.64, printed pp.580–581 (descent assertion); the finite-support proof below is written by the agent, not the Morita-equivalence proof in A.64.

proof.text: To prove injectivity, choose a $k$-basis $B_0$ of $W_0$ and extend its image in $M$ to a $k$-basis $B$ of $M$, using [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-basis-through-vector] twice. The image is $k$-linearly independent because $W_0\hookrightarrow M$ is an injective subspace inclusion. By [def-weil-vector-space-scalar-extension], the tensors $b\otimes1$ for $b\in B_0$ form an $L$-basis of $W_0\otimes_kL$, while their images under $F$ are part of the $L$-basis $b\otimes1$ for $b\in B$ of $M_L$. If $F(z)=0$, express $z$ as a finite combination of the former basis; independence of the latter forces every coefficient to be zero, so $z=0$. Thus $F$ is injective; together with its image $W$, it is the claimed isomorphism onto $W$. All coordinate sums used here are finite even when either vector space or the Galois extension is infinite.
